result:
{
  "thinking": "Maya wants to swap the fish for a butterfly, and Leo hasn't locked anything yet. I'm the Eng, so I should say what a butterfly means for the run before the design gets locked.",
  "say": "Hang on, before Leo locks, a butterfly's fine from my side. One outline, start at the head, and it splits into the two wings. The antennae are the risky bit. They're thin and easy to knock, and they only fall if they're joined to the head. Make them proper strokes, not tiny dots, and have them leave the head at a similar angle to the wing lines. And if we keep the fish, my tail-fork point still stands.",
  "to": "everyone",
  "eagerness": 6,
  "point": [6, 5],
  "do": "stop",
  "review": "Butterfly works if it's one connected outline: start at the head, run splits into the two wings, which mirror. Antennae must be joined strokes off the head, not separate pieces, and long enough to survive (not tiny). Keep their angle within about 40 degrees of the head line they leave from. Avoid sharp corners where the wings meet the body. If we keep the fish: tail fork as short joined branches, no sharp turns, skip the eye.",
  "notes": "Round 1. Leo's original draft: fish facing right, start at top tail tip. Maya proposed swapping to a butterfly: wings as big outline, antennae as telltale details. My review gave: butterfly OK if one connected outline from head, antennae joined and not tiny, angles within 40 degrees, no sharp wing-body corners. Fish fallback: tail fork as short joined branches, skip eye. Waiting for Leo to decide and lock. Once locked, I'll dry-run the joins before building the Eng part (antennae and wing-body joins are the weak spots)."
}
